source.title_on_document: Can Gen AI Improve Creativity in Students with Low Academic Performance? A Quasi-Experimental Study Based on Chinese Samples

supplement.where: In-article Appendices A-C at https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/21582440261449529, included in the saved publisher HTML text. No local PDF exists; no separate external supplement is identified.
supplement.holds: Appendix A, Table A1: intervention activities. Appendix B, Table B1 and worked example: creativity coding. Appendix C, Table C1: Levene tests and degrees of freedom. Creativity means/SDs, F tests, p values, and partial eta squared are in main-text Tables 2-3; mixed-model F tests are in Results, Creativity Test Results. No additional standard-error or confidence-interval tables are identified.

paper_design_summary: Three intact 11th-grade Engineering classes at a Shanghai secondary vocational school received ChatGLM, ChatGLM plus structured teacher support, or conventional project-based instruction with web-search access during an Innovation Training course (Methods, Intervention Design; Participants; Procedures). Although the authors call the study quasi-experimental, they explicitly report random assignment of entire classes to conditions (Methods, Procedures, Phase I). Pre/post divergent-thinking responses were coded for fluency, originality, elaboration, and flexibility; test-time AI access is not specified (Methods, Measurements; Appendix B).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Three intact classes were randomly assigned to EG1, EG2, and CG in the students' ordinary course. Treatment assignment was between classes; outcomes were measured pre/post. Separately, the school had randomly allocated students to classes at enrollment. field_rct follows the explicit treatment-assignment statement, although the authors label the design quasi-experimental.
assignment.quote: Three entire classes were randomly assigned to the control group, experimental group 1, and experimental group 2.
assignment.locator: Methods, Procedures, Phase I (class assignment to conditions); Methods, Participants (earlier school allocation to classes); Discussion, Limitations and Conclusion (quasi-experimental label and intact-class limitation).

arms.name: EG1: ChatGLM
arms.description: ChatGLM-supported autonomous project-based learning with little teacher intervention in exploration (Methods, Intervention Design; Appendix A, Table A1). Analyzed n is the Table 2 group-header count.

arms.name: EG2: ChatGLM + teacher structure support
arms.description: ChatGLM plus teacher structure support: task objectives, process/task sheets, guiding questions, templates, and personalized feedback (Methods, Intervention Design; Appendix A, Table A1). Analyzed n is the Table 2 group-header count.

arms.name: CG: conventional instruction + web search
arms.description: Conventional project-based instruction without ChatGLM, using teacher explanations, cases, ordinary tools, and web-search access (Methods, Intervention Design; Procedures, Phase I; Appendix A, Table A1). Analyzed n is the Table 2 group-header count.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions, attrition, or missing-data handling are stated. Tables 2 and 4 label groups N = 26, 22, and 27, consistent with the stated total of 75. Appendix C, Table C1 prints df1 = 2 and df2 = 51 for creativity, and df1 = 2 and df2 = 60 for psychological perceptions; these do not align with the table-header Ns. The reported Ns are retained without deriving alternative counts. No separate people count explicitly at randomization is given, so n_randomized is null.
participants.who: 11th-grade students, ages 16 to 17, in the same Engineering major at one medium-level secondary vocational school; classes followed the same curriculum and were taught by the same teacher (Methods, Participants).
participants.quote: A total of 75 11th-grade students from 3 intact classes in a secondary vocational school in Shanghai were selected for this study.
participants.locator: Methods, Participants; Tables 2 and 4, group N headers; Appendix C, Table C1.

ai_tool.how_used: Students used ChatGLM to brainstorm project themes, perform SWOT analyses, design consumer surveys, summarize market information, generate brand ideas, draft marketing/entrepreneurial plans, and polish presentations. EG1 selected AI content with little teacher intervention; EG2 received additional teacher scaffolding and feedback. The intelligent-body graphic in Figure 2 is absent from the saved text (Methods, Intervention Design; Appendix A, Table A1).

task.description: The intervention involved business-plan development in an Innovation Training course. Scored tasks were separate open-ended divergent-thinking tests inspired by ATTA, not original ATTA questions: innovative strategies to make daily life more convenient at pretest, and to build an international child-friendly city in Shanghai at posttest. The business plans themselves were not reported as scored creativity outcomes (Methods, Intervention Design; Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity; Appendix B).
task.duration: Each creativity test lasted 15 minutes. The study lasted 12 weeks: Phase I preparation/pretest, 2 weeks; Phase II intervention, 9 weeks at 90 minutes per week; Phase III post-test, 1 week (Methods, Procedures; Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity).

outcomes.name: Ability of fluency
outcomes.measure_detail: Manually coded count of distinct, relevant, non-repetitive ideas per participant; each valid idea receives one point. Irrelevant and repeated ideas do not count (Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity; Appendix B, Table B1). Two researchers scored pre/post-test responses; agreement coefficients were all higher than 0.76 (Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity). The omnibus time × group result is F = 7.274, p = .002, partial η² = 0.222 (Table 2). A robustness linear mixed-effects model with class as a random factor reports F = 5.895, p <.01 for this interaction (Results, Creativity Test Results). This is a robustness variant of the same outcome; pairwise mixed-model estimates, standard errors, and confidence intervals are not reported. Question and AI availability are null because test-time ChatGLM permission is not stated.
outcomes.delay: Assessed in the later Phase III post-test phase (1 week), after the Phase II intervention (9 weeks). Exact time from the last intervention session or AI use to the test is not stated; the phase duration is not a reported delay in days (Methods, Procedures).

outcomes.name: Ability of originality
outcomes.measure_detail: Manual count of infrequently generated ideas per participant, with frequency evaluated relative to the full sample. Methods uses less than 5% of the sample; Appendix B uses no more than 5% of participants. This is participant originality, not diversity across people (Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity; Appendix B, Table B1). Two researchers scored pre/post-test responses; agreement coefficients were all higher than 0.76 (Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity). The omnibus time × group result is F = 5.805, p = .005, partial η² = 0.185 (Table 2). A robustness linear mixed-effects model with class as a random factor reports F = 4.198, p <.05 for this interaction (Results, Creativity Test Results). This is a robustness variant of the same outcome; pairwise mixed-model estimates, standard errors, and confidence intervals are not reported. Question and AI availability are null because test-time ChatGLM permission is not stated.

outcomes.name: Ability of flexibility
outcomes.measure_detail: Manual count of distinct conceptual categories in one participant's responses. Methods refers to a pre-generated category list; Appendix B describes trained raters categorizing ideas and resolving categories through verification and discussion. Variety within a person's ideas is flexibility, not diversity across people (Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity; Appendix B, Table B1). Two researchers scored pre/post-test responses; agreement coefficients were all higher than 0.76 (Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity). The omnibus time × group result is F = 6.089, p = .004, partial η² = 0.193 (Table 2). A robustness linear mixed-effects model with class as a random factor reports F = 5.069, p <.01 for this interaction (Results, Creativity Test Results). This is a robustness variant of the same outcome; pairwise mixed-model estimates, standard errors, and confidence intervals are not reported. Question and AI availability are null because test-time ChatGLM permission is not stated.

company_involvement.description: No company role in conducting or funding the study is reported. Author affiliations are academic/research institutes; funders are Chinese public research agencies; authors declare no potential conflicts. eligibility.reason: Methods, Procedures, Phase I explicitly states that the three entire classes were randomly assigned to the AI conditions and control, supporting class-level field randomization despite the quasi-experimental label. Methods, Participants states 75 students; Table 2 reports analyzed arm Ns of 26, 22, and 27. Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity and Appendix B document four scores coded from participant-produced responses. All three screening criteria are met as reported. Appendix C degrees of freedom conflict with reported Ns, only three classes were assigned, and test-time AI access is unspecified; these limitations are retained for audit.

one_line_finding: In the reported 75-student sample, ChatGLM plus teacher structure support showed greater pre/post gains than conventional instruction on fluency, originality, elaboration, and flexibility (p = .001, .001, <.001, and .004), while ChatGLM alone showed no clear advantage (Tables 2-3).
open_questions: Was ChatGLM available during either 15-minute creativity test, especially the Phase III post-test? The text says testing followed the intervention but does not state that AI was removed; question and ai_available_when_produced are null rather than guessed (Methods, Procedures; Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity).

How do Tables 2 and 4 analyzed Ns (EG1 26, EG2 22, CG 27) reconcile with Appendix C, Table C1 denominator degrees of freedom of 51 for creativity and 60 for psychological perceptions? No exclusions or outcome-specific sample sizes are explained.

What procedure randomized the intact classes, and how should precision be handled with only three classes? The explicit randomization statement supports field_rct coding, although the paper calls its design quasi-experimental and cautions about class-level differences (Methods, Procedures, Phase I; Discussion, Limitations and Conclusion).
Was elaboration scored per response containing details or per individual detail instance? Methods and the Appendix B worked example use the former, but Table B1 describes the latter.

notes: Screened against the entire saved publisher HTML text, including references and Appendices A-C, on 2026-10-09. The retrieval record has pdf_path = null, so all locators are sections/tables and pages remain null. Figure captions/placeholders survive, but graphics are absent. source.supplement.exists = yes refers to included in-article appendices; in_this_pdf = false means no PDF is on file, not that appendices are missing from the saved text. Outcome inventory: Tables 2-3, Figure 5 caption, and Appendix B report fluency, originality, elaboration, and flexibility, included as four outcomes with three contrasts each. Tables 1, 4, and 5 and Figure 6 caption report five self-reported psychological variables: learning attitude, flow experience, perceived creativity, self-efficacy, and cognitive load. They are excluded from outcomes because they are not scored on creative output. Appendix C gives homogeneity diagnostics for these same nine variables, not new substantive outcomes; Appendix A describes activities. No overall creativity composite or across-person diversity outcome is reported. category_count denotes manually coded counts, not an automated creativity judge. No unique primary outcome or preregistration is specified. timing = delayed denotes the separate Phase III post-intervention assessment phase, not a confirmed retention interval; the exact delay is not reported. Question and AI availability remain null under the instruction not to guess, as neither after_ai nor with_ai can be confirmed. Partial eta squared values are copied as reported standardized effects; no effect sizes, changes, or standard errors have been computed. Table 3 tests compare pre/post trajectories, not posttest-only means. The control explicitly had web-search access, supporting ai_vs_active; EG2 versus EG1 adds teacher structure support with the same ChatGLM, coded ai_design. Class-random-factor mixed-model F tests are retained as robustness variants in measure_detail; pairwise mixed-model uncertainty estimates are not given. Data availability statement says data can be provided on request to the corresponding author; no data repository or code URL is supplied.
